paras: The threatened lynching of Frederick W. Williams took place on the night of August 22, 1903, in Washington, D.C., when white men in the poolroom of James Stevens' saloon at Eighth and E Streets northwest seized Williams, a Black man accused of stabbing a white tinner, Nelson Pixton, while a crowd shouted for him to be lynched. The saloon's proprietor hid Williams in a back room until police arrived and arrested him, and he was later convicted of assault with a dangerous weapon, with a jury recommendation of mercy. Only The Washington Times reported the threat, under the deck "Lynching Was Threatened."

Pixton, a tinner who lived near Schultzer Park northwest, had spent most of the afternoon with five or six friends in the poolroom at the rear of Stevens' saloon, and they were playing pool when Williams, described as "colored," came in. An argument followed in which the white men and Williams called each other names; Williams said the white men began it, while they blamed him.

Blows were exchanged and Williams was knocked down, after which, according to witnesses quoted by the Times, he stabbed Pixton in the left side, turned the knife in the wound, and wiped it and put it in his pocket. Pixton's friends then grabbed Williams and tried to drag him outside the saloon. Stevens intervened, took Williams from them and put him in a back room, where Williams protested that he had used the knife only in self-defense.

By the Times's account, Williams's bleeding nose, his blood mingling with Pixton's, further angered "the gathering mob," which shouted "Lynch the bloody nigger" again and again until the arrival of the police quieted it. Policemen Levi and Wolfe found a knife like the one witnesses described in Williams's pocket and took him to the First Precinct station, where a charge was entered against him. At the Emergency Hospital, physicians found a three-inch wound just below Pixton's heart and a puncture of the stomach, sewed up both wounds and kept him in a ward.

On August 24 the Police Court committed Williams to jail without bond to await the result of Pixton's injuries, after Prosecutor Given directed that he be held without bail. Indicted for assault with a dangerous weapon, Williams was found guilty in Criminal Court No. 2 on November 1, 1904, but the jury added "a strong recommendation for the mercy of the court." No report of Pixton's death, of Williams's sentence, or of any action against the men who seized him appears in the coverage.

The Washington Times gave the fullest account on August 23, under the headline "Nelson Pixton, White Is Stabbed by a Negro" and the decks "Lynching Was Threatened" and "Witnesses Infuriated by the Cold-Blooded Attack, But Bartender Intervened." Its story credited the proprietor's "prompt action" with saving Williams from lynching and passed on witnesses' description of the stabbing as "particularly vicious and cold-blooded," while also reporting Williams's claim of self-defense. The Evening Star's brief notice the next day, headed "Committed to Jail," said only that the men "had some trouble," and neither it nor the Star's 1904 report of the verdict mentioned the crowd. All of the coverage found came from these two white Washington dailies; no report in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Frederick W. Williams
bases: Pixton's friends seized Williams, accused of stabbing a white man, and tried to drag him outside while a crowd shouted for him to be lynched; no one was killed, so this is a threatened lynching (A1).

Williams was seized by Pixton's friends (five or six were in the room) and a crowd called for his lynching over the stabbing, but the proprietor hid him and police arrested him, so no one was killed (A1, A2); it was a threatened lynching only.
The stabbing, arrest and conviction are reported in two Washington papers (A1, A2, A6), but the seizure of Williams and the shouts of 'Lynch' appear only in the Washington Times (A1).

accounts.label: White witnesses (Washington Times)
accounts.gist: The white men blamed Williams for the quarrel, and witnesses described the stabbing as vicious and cold-blooded, with Williams turning the knife and pocketing it.

accounts.label: Williams
accounts.gist: Williams said the white men started the quarrel and that he used the knife only in self-defense after being knocked down.

accounts.label: Court record
accounts.gist: Williams was committed without bond, indicted for assault with a dangerous weapon, and convicted with a jury recommendation of mercy.

framing.detail: The Times headlined 'Nelson Pixton, White Is Stabbed by a Negro' and 'Lynching Was Threatened', relayed witnesses' 'cold-blooded' description, credited the proprietor with preventing a lynching, and reported Williams's self-defense claim.
The Evening Star ran brief court notices ('Committed to Jail', 'Williams Found Guilty') that said nothing of the crowd.

conflicts.note: The Times reports both claims and does not resolve them; the jury's recommendation of mercy (A6) is not explained.
